strengths: Well-motivated framework: Addresses two critical challenges in MLLM-based embodied AI—geometric adaptability (through selective 3D injection) and physical execution feasibility (through embodiment-aware constraints).

Innovative components: (1) The Task-Adaptive Gated Router (TAGR) dynamically regulates the injection of 3D positional encodings based on the task description and scene complexity. (2) The Task- and Embodiment-aware GRPO (TE-GRPO) incorporates robotic constraints (kinematics, reachability) using RL with a progressive curriculum.

Comprehensive evaluation: The paper demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on a wide range of benchmarks (7 out of 8 public 2D/3D embodied reasoning datasets) and provides end-to-end simulator evaluations for navigation and mobile manipulation tasks.
Physical deployment: The proposed planner is successfully deployed and validated on a wheeled dual-arm physical robot platform, demonstrating real-world feasibility.
Highly detailed appendix: Contains extensive qualitative examples across multiple tasks, clear training configurations, and a comprehensive breakdown of the training dataset.
weaknesses: Lack of efficiency/latency analysis for the TAGR module: The paper claims that selective 3D grounding avoids unnecessary computation. However, there is no quantitative comparison of training/inference latency, token counts, or GFLOPs to demonstrate how much computation is saved when the 3D gate is deactivated.

Unclear simulation overhead in TE-GRPO training: The reward function utilizes `EvalExec` to validate trajectories against kinematic and environment boundaries in the simulator. The authors should clarify how computationally expensive it is to run these simulator checks in-the-loop during reinforcement learning updates and how they scale with group size.

Heavy reliance on in-house benchmarks: Several evaluations (Where2Go, Where2Fit, Where2Approach, Where2Grasp) are custom benchmarks. Although detailed in the appendix, comparisons with established open-source benchmarks would strengthen the validation.

Minor typos and formatting errors: For example, 'More rencent approaches' on page 3, 'OminiEVA' on page 3, and the hanging text 'complex 3D environments.huozh' at the end of Appendix A.2.2 on page 20.

strengths: The paper addresses two highly relevant and critical bottlenecks in VLM-based embodied planning: the rigidity of 3D feature integration (Geometric Adaptability Gap) and the lack of physical constraints consideration (Embodiment Constraint Gap).

The proposed Task-Adaptive Gated Router (TAGR) is a clever design that dynamically controls the injection of 3D spatial priors based on task instruction semantics and scene complexity, preventing unnecessary computation and noise in 2D-dominant tasks.

The Task- and Embodiment-aware GRPO (TE-GRPO) algorithm successfully bridges high-level semantic reasoning with low-level execution feasibility by leveraging a curriculum-based reward scheduling scheme.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation is presented across 8 public 2D/3D benchmarks, alongside 4 proposed primitive benchmarks, showing consistent state-of-the-art results even when compared to much larger models (e.g., GPT-4o, Robobrain-32B).
Strong evidence of physical reality grounding through simulator-based end-to-end testing and real-world robotic deployment on a wheeled dual-arm platform.
weaknesses: Details regarding how the baseline general models (like GPT-4o and Gemini-2.5-Pro) were evaluated on the in-house benchmarks are slightly unclear. Clarification on whether they received similar depth representations or coordinate mappings would ensure a fairer comparison.

The programmatic pipeline for the execution reward ($r^{embod}$) inside the TE-GRPO loop is not fully detailed. It would be highly beneficial to explain the exact simulator setup (e.g., PyBullet, Isaac Sim) and the computational overhead of invoking kinematic/collision checks during reinforcement learning.

Since the parameters of the TAGR module are frozen after the pretraining stage, there is a risk of routing misalignment on highly novel out-of-distribution tasks. The paper would be stronger with an ablation study or discussion on the failure cases/generalization limits of the gating module.
Minor typos are present in the text, such as referring to the module as 'TGGR' instead of 'TAGR' on page 9.

strengths: Addresses two critical and highly relevant bottlenecks in MLLM-based embodied AI: spatial-geometric adaptability and the physical feasibility gap.
The Task-Adaptive Gated Router (TAGR) is a well-designed module that dynamically routes 3D spatial priors based on contextual demands and scene complexity, avoiding unnecessary computation and noise.

Introduces TE-GRPO, an embodiment-aware reinforced fine-tuning strategy with a progressive curriculum that successfully guides the model to respect physical robot constraints (reachability, kinematics, obstacles).
Extensive and comprehensive evaluation spanning 2D/3D visual QA benchmarks, custom primitive skills, online simulations, and real-world dual-arm robot deployments.
weaknesses: The performance gain of the dynamic gated router (TAGR) over hard-coded 3D integration in Table 1 is quite marginal (+1.22% on average), and it even underperforms on ScanQA. To make this contribution stronger, the authors should provide computational complexity analyses (e.g., reduction in FLOPs, inference latency) when the 3D encoder pathway is gated off.

The model is trained on a massive hybrid dataset of 5.2 million samples. It remains unclear how much of the final performance boost over baselines is driven by this huge scale of high-quality data versus the proposed architectural and RL contributions. An ablation study controlling for dataset size is missing.

The details regarding the online simulator-in-the-loop reward calculation ($r^{embod}$) during TE-GRPO training are sparse. It is unclear which simulator is integrated, how collision/kinematics checks are executed efficiently in parallel during GRPO rollouts, and what the associated computational overhead is.
Minor presentation issues and typos are present, such as 'OMINI-SUPERVISED' in the title of Section 3.3.1 and the truncated text '.huozh' at the end of Section A.2.2.
